summary: Specifies procedures for registering charsets with IANA, which is needed because MIME and other protocols can use many different charsets and need to label them. It is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: Computers use many ways to turn letters into numbers. This sets the rules for getting a new one added to the official list.

questions: how to register a charset with iana
what is the difference between a charset and a character encoding scheme
how long does charset registration take
subtitle: The rules and review steps for getting a character set name and number added to the IANA charset registry.

tldr.problem: MIME and other Internet protocols can use many different charsets, so being able to label them with agreed names is essential.
tldr.mechanism: A proposer posts the registration to a mailing list for two weeks of public review, a charset reviewer approves or rejects it within two weeks, and IANA then registers it and assigns a MIBenum value.
tldr.outcome: Registration only associates names with a charset and says whether it suits MIME text. It does not endorse the charset. The RFC obsoletes RFC 2278.

facts.label: MIBenum display name
facts.value: Starts with cs, at most 40 characters

today: RFC 2978 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 19) and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It obsoleted RFC 2278.

sections.title: Charset Terminology
sections.content:
A charset is a method of converting a sequence of octets into a sequence of characters, optionally with extra control information such as directionality indicators. The conversion in the other direction need not be unconditional or unambiguous. The definition behind a charset name must fully specify the mapping, and external profiling information may not be used to decide the exact mapping.

The RFC also defines two building blocks. A Coded Character Set (CCS) is a one-to-one mapping from abstract characters to integers, such as ISO 10646, US-ASCII or the ISO-8859 series. A Character Encoding Scheme (CES) maps one or more coded character sets to octet sequences; UTF-8, for example, applies only to ISO 10646.

A historical note explains that MIME once said "character set" for simple schemes like US-ASCII, and the term changed to "charset" because multi-octet encodings and switching techniques make the situation more complex. Requirement words such as MUST and SHOULD follow RFC 2119.
sections.eli5: A charset is a rulebook that says which bunch of numbers means which letters. The rulebook has to be complete, with no guessing.

sections.title: What a Charset Must Have to Register
sections.content:
A registered charset MUST meet the definition above. Charsets for MIME text content types must follow the restrictions in RFC 2045, and every registration MUST note whether it is suitable for MIME text. A charset built from a CCS and a CES MUST include those definitions or cite them elsewhere. Every registered charset MUST have a stable, openly available specification; registering one without it is forbidden.

The mechanism is not for designing entirely new charsets, because the process lacks adequate review. Only charsets defined by other processes and standards bodies, or profiles and combinations of them, are eligible. Things better thought of as a transfer encoding, a media type or a collection of other entities cannot be registered; HTML is the RFC's example of a media type.

A charset should be registered only if it adds significant functionality valuable to a large community, or documents existing practice in a large community. Charsets registered for the second reason should be marked as limited or specialized use and used in Internet messages only with prior bilateral agreement.
sections.eli5: You can only sign up a code that already exists and is written down for anyone to read. You cannot invent a brand new one here, and it should be useful to lots of people.

sections.title: Names and MIBenum Values
sections.content:
Every registered charset gets one or more names. If there are several, one primary name MUST be identified and the others are aliases, with the primary name preferred. Each name MUST identify a single charset and be valid as a MIME content type charset parameter value.

Each charset also needs a name that gives a display string for its MIBenum value, as defined in the Printer MIB (RFC 1759). Such a name MUST begin with cs and contain no more than 40 characters of printable US-ASCII, including the prefix. Only one cs name may be assigned to a charset; if none is given, IANA assigns an alias made by putting cs in front of the primary name.

Charsets registered for the text media type need a primary name that fits the stricter syntax of MIME encoded-words and extended parameter values (RFC 2047, RFC 2184). The RFC gives an ABNF for it. Each charset also gets a unique integer MIBenum value, which IANA assigns at registration; the registrant does not choose it.
sections.eli5: Each code gets an official name, maybe some nicknames, and a number handed out by the list keeper. You cannot pick your own number.

sections.title: The Registration Procedure
sections.content:
This is an administrative procedure rather than a formal standards process, meant to allow community comment and sanity checking without long delays. There are three steps.

  1. Present to the community. Send the proposed registration to the ietf-charsets@iana.org mailing list. Posting starts a two week public review. Proposed charsets are not registered and must not be used; the x- prefix from RFC 2045 can be used until registration is done.
  2. Charset reviewer. After the two weeks, once the proposer is convinced consensus is reached, the application goes to IANA and the charset reviewer, who is appointed by the IETF Applications Area Director(s). The reviewer approves or rejects it, and must decide and post the decision to the list within two weeks. Rejection may follow significant objections. For an important and controversial case, a last call may go to the full IETF. The reviewer may recommend standards track processing. Decisions can be appealed to the IESG.
  3. IANA registration. If the registration passed review or won an appeal to the IESG, IANA registers the charset, assigns a MIBenum value and makes the registration available.
sections.eli5: First you show your idea to everyone for two weeks. Then one referee says yes or no. If it is yes, the list keeper writes it in the book and gives it a number.

sections.title: The Registration Template
sections.content:
Proposals are sent using a template addressed to ietf-charsets@iana.org with the subject Registration of new charset [names]. Its fields are: charset name, charset aliases, suitability for use in MIME text, published specification(s), ISO 10646 equivalency table, additional information, a contact person and email address, and intended usage.

The specification MUST be openly available and accurately describe what is registered, and if the charset is composed of CCSs and a CES, those must be included or referenced. A URI for an ISO 10646 equivalency table SHOULD be provided. Intended usage is one of COMMON, LIMITED USE or OBSOLETE.
sections.eli5: It is a form with blanks: the name, nicknames, where the rules are written, who to ask, and whether it is common, rare or old.

sections.title: Publication and What Registration Means
sections.content:
Charset registrations may be published in RFCs, but that is not required. Registration does not imply endorsement, approval or recommendation by IANA, the IESG or the IETF, or certification that the specification is adequate. The RFC expects separate applicability statements to recommend particular charsets for particular applications. Registrations SHOULD include a mapping into ISO 10646 where feasible.

Registered charsets are posted in a file on the IANA FTP area and listed in the periodically issued "Assigned Numbers" RFC (then RFC 1700). The description may also be sent to the RFC Editor for publication as an Informational RFC.
sections.eli5: Being on the list just means the name is official. It does not mean the experts think the code is a good one.

sections.title: Security and Changes From RFC 2278
sections.content:
The RFC says the procedure is not known to raise security considerations appreciably different from those already present in the protocols that use registered charsets.

It obsoletes RFC 2278. The changes are that including a mapping to ISO 10646 is now recommended for all registered charsets, and the template now includes that mapping and a place to say whether the charset suits MIME text.
sections.eli5: Signing up a name does not add new dangers. The newer rules just ask you to also say how your code maps to the big universal one.

messages.label: Post proposal
messages.note: Starts a two week public review.

messages.label: Submit application
messages.note: After two weeks, once consensus is reached.

messages.label: Post decision
messages.note: Within two weeks; appealable to the IESG.

messages.label: Approved
messages.note: IANA registers it and assigns a MIBenum value.
